title: Seven runs and a spring
hookLine: Hajar runs seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, and water springs by the baby's feet
last: THEN WE WILL NOT BE LOST.

cards: To the door and back. To the door and back. A parent pacing a hallway at three in the morning, because moving is the only thing left to do.
That's where we find Hajar. The dates are gone. The water skin is empty.
She is thirsty, the baby is thirsty, and Isma'il is crying and twisting on the ground. She can't bear to watch. So she climbs the nearest hill and looks for anyone at all.
Nobody. She runs down, across the valley floor, and up the hill on the other side. Nobody.

teach.b: The same hadith in Bukhari tells it. The first hill is Safa, the second is Marwa. She goes back and forth between them seven times, climbing, looking, running the low stretch between.
On the seventh, she hears a voice. She says: you've made me hear you; if you can help, help.

And there, by the baby, is an angel, striking the ground with his heel, and water comes up out of the dry earth. She hurries to hold it in, scooping sand around it into a little basin, filling her skin.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, telling this story long afterward, adds a line of pure tenderness: may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il.

teach.h: IF SHE HAD LEFT IT, A STREAM.
teach.b: If she had left it alone, Zamzam would have been a flowing stream.

That spring still flows in Mecca, in the grounds of the great mosque, where pilgrims drink from it and carry it home in bottles for the people who couldn't come. Where the name comes from, nobody knows for certain.
A story people tell says Hajar called out zam, zam, hold still, gather, as she held the water in. Take that as a story, not a record. And the running didn't stop with her.
The Prophet said that's why people go between the two hills.
Pilgrims at Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwa seven times, and in one marked stretch the walk quickens, as hers did.
The Qur'an calls Safa and Marwa among the signs of Allah. So a rite of the pilgrimage retraces a mother's search: not her calm, her running. It honors the searching as much as the finding.

how: During Hajj and Umrah, pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, a rite called sa'y, and drink Zamzam water, which pilgrims often carry home to share with family and friends.

practice: If there's room where you are, stand and take seven steps one way, then seven back, seven times, slowly; if you can't stand, trace it with a finger on your knee.
With each length, think of one thing you're still looking for, still hoping for, still running toward. If you pray, make a small prayer on each length; if not, just count, and feel your feet.

wordCard.voice: Zamzam. The spring that came up by Isma'il's feet in the dry valley, still flowing in Mecca today.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the spring in Mecca. its origin is uncertain; one story links it to "zam," hold still, gather.

carryVoice: Your line: keep running; the water comes. It came on her seventh run, not her first. Forty days.
